# SuperDB

> SuperDB is an open-source analytics database and command-line query engine
> built on the algebraic data model, which unifies relational tables and JSON
> in one type system of records, unions, arrays, sets, and maps. Its query
> language, SuperSQL, is a pipe SQL that is aspirationally backward-compatible
> with PostgreSQL.

Key facts for writing SuperDB queries and commands:

- The `super` command queries files, URLs, and standard input directly, e.g.,
  `super -c "from logs.json | where status==200 | count() by host | sort count desc"`.
  `super db` manages and queries a persistent database of tables.
- SuperSQL queries can be written in SQL (`SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY`),
  as a pipeline of operators separated by `|`, or a mix of both.
  A query may begin with `from` or with any operator.
- Data in SuperDB, called super-structured data, is strongly typed without a
  schema: every value carries its own type (records, arrays, sets, maps,
  unions, options, enums, errors, fusion types, and named types), so data of
  different shapes can coexist, and queries are statically type checked
  against the types of the data.
- SUP is the human-readable text format and is a superset of JSON.
  BSUP is the binary format, in row or columnar form.
  `super` also reads and writes JSON, NDJSON, CSV, TSV, Parquet, Arrow IPC,
  line, and Zeek formats.
- Use `-s` for SUP output and `-j` for JSON output; the default output is
  SUP on a terminal and BSUP otherwise.

Common idioms:

- `values <expr>` emits the value of an expression for each input value and is
  the pipe counterpart of `SELECT`. Its results need not be records, e.g.,
  `values {id, kind:type}` or `values dimensions`. The `values` keyword is
  optional.
- A field that some values lack must be handled explicitly: `x.ok()` turns a
  missing field or an error into `none`, `a?.b` stops at `none`, and `a ?? b`
  supplies a default, e.g., `values dimensions.radius.ok() ?? 0`.
  `is_ok(x)` tests whether a value is present.
- A type assertion `x.(T)` is `x` when `x` has type `T` and `none` otherwise,
  e.g., `values this.(Circle)`. A cast is written `x::T`.
- `aggregate fuse(this)` shows the one type that describes all of the input,
  and `values typeof(this)` shows the type of each value.
- `unnest <array>` emits the elements of an array as separate values.
- A "no such field" or "field may be missing" error is a compile-time type
  error, not a transient failure. Fix the query (correct the field name, or
  handle the missing case with `ok()`, `?.`, or `??`) rather than retrying it.

Avoid outdated syntax from earlier versions (when the project was called Zed):

- The command is `super`, not `zq` or `zed`, and the formats are SUP and BSUP,
  not ZSON, ZNG, VNG, CSUP, or JSUP.
- Use `values`, not `yield`, and `unnest`, not `over`.
- Use `fuse`, not `blend`. `superfuse` produces fusion types, and `defuse()`
  and `superdefuse()` undo them.
- Use `ok()` and `is_ok()`, not `has()`, `missing()`, or `quiet()`.
- A database has tables, not pools, and a database is selected with
  `super db attach`, not `super db auth` or `super db login`.
- The instant-in-time type is `timestamp`, not `time`, and the non-aggregate
  maximum and minimum functions are `greatest()` and `least()`.
- In SUP, sets are written `set[...]`, maps are written `map{...}`, the none
  value is `none`, and a named type is declared with a `type` statement,
  e.g., `type port=uint16`.

## Getting Started

- [Introduction](https://superdb.org/intro.html): What SuperDB is and the ideas behind it
- [The Algebraic Data Model](https://superdb.org/adm.html): Why relational tables and JSON are both special cases of one algebraic type system
- [Installation](https://superdb.org/getting-started/install.html): Installing `super` with Homebrew, prebuilt binaries, or from source
- [TL;DR](https://superdb.org/getting-started/tldr.html): A quick tour of SuperDB
- [Hello World](https://superdb.org/getting-started/hello-world.html): A first query
- [Playground](https://superdb.org/getting-started/playground.html): Running examples in the browser

## CLI

- [super](https://superdb.org/command/super.html): The `super` command and its options
- [Input](https://superdb.org/command/input.html): Reading files, URLs, and standard input
- [Output](https://superdb.org/command/output.html): Output formats and options
- [Formats](https://superdb.org/command/formats.html): Supported input and output formats
- [super db](https://superdb.org/command/db.html): Creating, loading, branching, and querying a database, and serving it over HTTP
- [MCP server](https://superdb.org/command/db.html#super-db-mcp): Running a Model Context Protocol server for AI agents with `super db mcp`

## SuperSQL

- [Overview](https://superdb.org/super-sql/intro.html): The SuperSQL language
- [Queries](https://superdb.org/super-sql/queries.html): Query structure, pipes, and scopes
- [Statements](https://superdb.org/super-sql/statements/intro.html): Scripts and the CREATE TABLE, CREATE SUPER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and INSERT statements
- [Declarations](https://superdb.org/super-sql/declarations/intro.html): Constants, types, functions, operators, queries, and pragmas
- [Expressions](https://superdb.org/super-sql/expressions/intro.html): Expression syntax, including casts and type assertions
- [Types](https://superdb.org/super-sql/types/intro.html): The super data model's types and SQL type names
- [Operators](https://superdb.org/super-sql/operators/intro.html): Pipe operators like `where`, `values`, `aggregate`, `sort`, `join`, `fork`, and `unnest`
- [SQL](https://superdb.org/super-sql/sql/intro.html): SQL clauses and PostgreSQL compatibility
- [Functions](https://superdb.org/super-sql/functions/intro.html): Built-in functions
- [Aggregate Functions](https://superdb.org/super-sql/aggregates/intro.html): Aggregate functions
- [Type Fusion](https://superdb.org/super-sql/type-fusion.html): Combining the varying types of messy data into one type

## Formats

- [Super Data Model](https://superdb.org/formats/model.html): The super data model, SuperDB's implementation of the algebraic data model
- [Super (SUP)](https://superdb.org/formats/sup.html): The human-readable text format
- [Super Binary (BSUP)](https://superdb.org/formats/bsup.html): The binary row and columnar format

## Database

- [Database](https://superdb.org/database/intro.html): Tables, branches, commits, and time travel
- [API](https://superdb.org/database/api.html): The HTTP API of `super db serve`

## Optional

- [Database Format](https://superdb.org/database/format.html): The storage layout of a database
- [Libraries](https://superdb.org/dev/libraries/intro.html): Go, Python, and JavaScript libraries
- [Integrations](https://superdb.org/dev/integrations/intro.html): Amazon S3 and Zeek
- [Blog: The Sum Type Hiding in Your JSON](https://superdb.org/blog/gharchive.html): Querying a day of GitHub Archive events and shaping them into a sum type
- [Blog: JSON Can't Tell a Map from a Record](https://superdb.org/blog/json-map-or-record.html): What JSON columns cost and how typed data avoids it
- [Blog: Algebraic Types, End to End](https://superdb.org/blog/end-to-end.html): Rust and TypeScript types that survive a round trip through SuperDB
- [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/superdb/super): Source code, issues, and releases
